comments.name: njdanielson
comments.body:
I am a 4th generation Albertan.
The separatist movement has been more robust in our province in the past.
In 1986, we had a separatist sitting in a seat in our provincial legislature.  He was elected in a rural riding not too far north of Calgary.  In 2025, the leader of the Separatist party (Republican Party of Alberta) came in 3rd in a by-election in that same area.  That is a bell weather for how strong the separatist sentiment is in the province.  80 percent of Albertans don’t want a referendum.  The premier has allowed the separatists to infiltrate her party and in fact, it is how she became leader of the party.  She doesn’t want to be removed so she is placating them with a referendum. 
Ms. Smith would never hold a referendum unless she knew that she would be the winner of it.   That is how she rolls.

comments.name: LaPine
comments.body: The separatist movement in Alberta makes as much sense as California, the 5th largest economy in the world, separating from the US.  It is billfold based, and I cannot be convinced otherwise.  Another alternative  madness would have the "Blue States" separating from the US; as they subsidize most of the "Red States' economically, but our motto translated is:  From many, one, i.e. unity, though trump is doing his best to negate that.  Throughout our history, different regions and States exhibited "boom' and "bust" times economically.  How soon we forget all the US Govt assistance to the "Dust Bowl" families during the depression, or the Agricultural support programs continuing to subsidize farmers, dairymen, cattle and livestock ranchers, wheat growers, etal. during periods of economic drought.  "From many, one.  An adult perspective would recognize the entire 250-yr period of ups and downs, not a snapshot of the present.  The Alberta tar sands boom won't last, it cannot if we are to survive as a species. Then where will you be?  BC is  running out of timber on a sustainable basis as the (free) old growth is liquidated.  What then?  That is where the concept of team becomes important.  Dismiss the "separatist" movements as narcissistic quackery they are.

My mom couldn’t even get a credit card without my dad signing off on it with the bank until 1974. Gloria Steinem and Bella Abzug were the background of my childhood growing up in the 70s, and their words were the music of dignity.

comments.name: TI85
comments.body: Thank you, Ms. Gloria. You and your sisters in the movement created a welcoming space in American society where I could thrive. Your fingerprints are all over my journey. I am an engineer because of "Take Our Daughters to Work Day." I am proud of being a woman because of the Ms. Foundation. The 2004 March on Washington reignited my advocacy flame. Inhaling The Kitchen Table Entrepreneurs book as an MBA student opened my eyes to how women lead in all environments. Through The White House Project, I gained my footing in politics. I can say literally, what would my life have been without you?

comments.name: Neil Bellinson

Few human beings have influenced human relationships to such a degree as Gloria Steinem.

comments.name: rachaelessss

comments.name: Birdie
comments.body:
I live in an apartment building on the Upper West Side, and on the Tenant committee we had one of those new vitamin infusion spa as a tenant in the commercial space.
 They created the most beautiful million-dollar space, beautifully appointed with all blonde wood; gorgeous. They lasted two years. 
They had no customers; people in the Upper West Side weren’t for the shenanigans of a vitamin IV spa. 
If you need IV vitamin supplementation or Prescription iron supplementation, your physician can provide that through the hospital or a physician’s office.
They are out of business, and now another big, empty, well-appointed space sits vacant on Columbus avenue. I hope a licensed physician takes over the space. It would be a perfectly lovely office space for any doctor.

comments.name: Fern
comments.body: I'm a retired nurse. I would NEVER allow any fluid into my veins anywhere but a hospital and that would require discussion. The possibilities for serious mistakes are astronomical! And you can't remove what has already gone in.

comments.name: Pinkie
comments.body: Very witty!  And very wise.  Anything can be monetized.

comments.name: Pickles
comments.body: If it sounds too good to be true, it is. Please stop this insanity. Give the $350 to someone in need. Please. Send it to Nepal.

comments.name: Patrick
comments.body:
Is there any scientific evidence that ingesting a large dose of vitamins is more beneficial than just swallowing one pill of each  vitamin?  And does entry directly into the blood stream have a greater, and more beneficial effect, than taking orally?

I suspect the answers are "no" ..., or, "not much".

What would PT Barnum have said about this? (Oh yeah, he already said it).

comments.name: Jane K
comments.body:
I started and ran IV’s in a hospital for more than 20 years.  There is no way I would want to sign up for an IV in some roadside spa.  

The potential for getting too much fluid and having a reaction to some weird ingredient is only one of the reasons why I would not sign up for a boutique IV.   It is cheaper and easier to drink a liter of gatorade after taking a handful of vitamins.  

I suppose I could work in one these places to make some extra money in retirement, but frankly, I would rather administer flu vaccines.  At least they will prevent illness.

articles.title: I Need an IV Drip to Recover From My IV Drip

comments.name: Fred
comments.body:
I resigned from the ACLU in protest after 44 years of membership because it had devolved from an organization devoted to free speech to one devoted to free speech only by those whom it liked, as well as, in the case of a leader of its LGBTQ rights division, one openly favoring censorship. Instead I joined FIRE, an organization that Mr. French once led.

But I am not optimistic about the future of free speech in America. Just the other day a Times reader commenting on an article declared that those opposed to a host of "progressive" causes were the enemy and deserved no free speech rights at all. This reader seems not to have been paying attention to the news, because in addition to claiming sanctimoniously to be defending free speech, our far-right government has been doing everything it can to destroy it.

It would help if at least a few political leaders of any stature defended free speech and meant it. To some of us, it is as important as cheap gas.

comments.name: Zakb
comments.body: Trump is a reality tv star.  the fact that he doesn't know the constitution and such reflects on the results of his education at Wharton amongst others.  He should know this stuff, I can give him the benefit of the doubt that he doesn't.  More troublesome is people like Rubio and members of congress who are politicians and many of them lawyers.  they should and do know better.  They are choosing to act against the constitution and laws they have been trained to understand and uphold.

comments.name: Charles Cohen
comments.body: Thank you for this piece.  It is a reminder that there is an "American way of life", and that it must be protected.  That includes protecting it from corruption by elected officials.

comments.name: HC
comments.body: Thank you Mr French for this well reasoned argument. Another aspect of this illegal arrest and detention is the overall effect it has on political dissent in general. Will we have to carry “papers” to prove our citizenship when engaging in protest? Will we get to the point where one tier of citizenship is more free to engage in certain forms of dissent than others?

comments.name: JMG
comments.body: “More broadly”, if there is not at least a ripple or a blue wave in November to staunch, if not thwart, the abuses in David French’s well written and reasoned article, the results will be academic: the Constitution in its entirety and Bill of Rights will not be worth the paper on which they’re written. They will have been discarded along with the rule of law under this and subsequent single-party dictatorship. Imagine Trump’s and his administration’s arrogance going forward with increasing criminality, and no doubt more SC complicity/empowerment and a renewed “mandate”. Game over.

comments.name: David Conn
comments.body:
Well said, David. And one other note to consider. Thanks to the link you provided, it was easy to read both the students' OpEd and the University's statement. The OpEd was simply wrong in declaring that response as "the automatic rejection, dismissive nature and condescending tone in the University’s statement."

The President's response was even-handed, considerate of all sides, and clear in denouncing both anti-Semitism and Islamophobia. 

And still, and crucially, all of this is what we should expect from university debates and none of it warrants the government actions we've seen. These are scary times, and we owe you gratitude, David, for highlighting it.

comments.body: Do we judge the art? Or do we judge the creator of the art? I totally understand the reluctance of many New Yorkers (Jewish and non-Jewish) to have the show. And yet, by cancelling the art, do we cancel ourselves?

comments.name: Jacob Kornman
comments.body: Would it not have been better if everyone had been able to make their own decision regarding this exhibition, by either visiting it or not?

comments.name: Carlyle T.
comments.body:
How many times have I as an accomplished artist wished to show at the Met and been so refused to as they say get to first base because of the politics and insane marriage of their curators  with gallery owners.
Reminding me in the day when artists carried a heavy portfolio case to be seen by galleries with the faith and hope for public exposure ,mayve a dollar or two whn a front desk person stated to me "We don't look at portfolio's we know who we want" I do shed few tears over this shows cancellation from a partly public funded museum whose curators remain that of a boss of a closed Union shop. "Go on ,no work here".

comments.name: D
comments.body:
The first sentence contains the crucial point.  The impetus for the exhibit was Anna Wintour, not some consensus from the curators or fashion community that Gaultier is the greatest working designer, has a unique vision, has elevated the artistic standards for fashion or meaningfully and uniquely integrated contemporary life into fashion. 
The article makes vague references to review by Board of Trustee groups but doesn’t identify them, not if formal approval was required or sought.  It does not say if there was any formal or informal discussion of Wintour’s financial or other dealings with Gaultier or the companies which would be given an enormous financial boost by being highlighted in the show. There is no mention of whether this is ever discussed or disclosed at the Museum.

comments.name: Nancy
comments.body: Anna Wintour overstepped. It's time for her to step away from the limelight. But she loves all the perks that come with that limelight. So many of the participants in the Met Gala don't look elegant or chic. They look like they're wearing Halloween costumes as the try to out-weird each other. And that goes for both the women and the men.

comments.name: John Greaves
comments.body: Galliano can apologize for his bigotry.  But, he is who he is. His hatred is so deep and long running, it strains credulity that somehow he's a changed man all of the sudden. His contrition is unworthy of belief.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: Putting this into perspective, After being tormented in a brasserie in Paris, Mr. Galliano lashed out and used colorful language, as one might do when feeling a little tipsy.  He has been on an endless apology tour for the past fifteen years since this happened, but that is not enough to show him mercy.  Since the war in Gaza began, more than 73,400 people have been killed and this is what our culture is outraged about.  This could have been a very special and rare and very beautiful, unifying  exhibition, and it has been spoiled over misplaced rage.  It is very disappointing that a wonderful opportunity like this was ruined and will not be enjoyed.  People really like holding onto grudges these days.  It's a sad state of affairs, and it spoils things for those of us who are able to forgive others. Anna Wintour has again demonstrated her bravery and loyalty in supporting one of the very greatest fashion designers ever, John Galliano.  Maybe someday, we can see this beautiful exhibition in New York City in a peaceful and celebratory way.

comments.name: Andrew (Andy) Anderson
comments.body: I don't know that there are any winners here. It was called a rare misstep, but it also appears that the process went through several levels of approval. Very unfortunate for all on both sides. Also, very unfortunate that anti-semitic crimes are on the rise in this great nation, and in NYC.

comments.name: M. David
comments.body: The false equivalence in this article is horrendous. In addition, there is no mention of why Ukraine is targeting the warehouses of Wildberries. If you read German news reporting (or perhaps other articles in the Times) you see it is because they provide material support for the Russian military. Russia has been bombarding civilian infrastructure since almost Day 1. Ukraine has now switched strategy to go after infrastructure that supports the military, like oil infrastructure, etc. The attacks Ukraine undertakes on "civilian" targets are more symbolic, it seems. While Russia has been butchering and slaughtering people since the very beginning. You are starting to sound like Scott Bessent. I'm not any kind of expert, but just generally following the news shows it's not a tit for tat -- that is the way Russia is framing it, it seems. Your reporting would be equivalent to saying the ICE watchers and protesters are now adopting tit for tat tactics with ICE: both sides are taking a hit. There are some similarities, sure. But your opening paragraph frames it as if it's just two sides pummeling each other in retaliation for what the other does. That is the way Putin frames it. I don't think, strategically, you've got it.

comments.name: Amy
comments.body:
What idiocy possessed the Western world to foster this catastrophe?And how is it that we don't learrn from our lessons and keep repeating our mistakes?

Remember when we were told that Western economic sanctions would bring Russia to its knees within a month? That was five years ago. 

But go back further. The Ukraine was was always foreseeable. Why? Because somehow Western powers ignored the fact that Russia would have to protect its own security interests.

So what did the West do? It poured gasoline on the flames, somehow persuading itself that more US and other troops on Russia's birders, more flaunting of weapons would cow Russia into submission.

Same old, same old.

And now we empower Zelensky to push Russia until it has no option but to take desperate measures that will send the world up in flames.

It's time we woke up to the idiocy of war, its effects on the global economy, on ordinary human beings and all the other creatures that habe the misfortune to share this planet with us. 

The obsession with war prevents us from facing the critical issues humanity is beginning to face on other fronts.

There is hope, but only if we abandon worn out ways of thinking based on might is right politics. We need new and  younger, more principled and visionary leaders who are not caught in old ways of thinking. (Many younger leaders are still captive to outworn politics and platitudes, but not all.) People whose first instinct is not money and power, but people and the planet.

comments.name: Bruno Corre
comments.body:
President Putin is a paranoid who has dragged his country into an irrational war.
Now, Russians are beginning to stir due to fuel shortages...
Obeying their dictator's orders, they torment Ukrainians in the most horrific ways and have been filling their own graveyards for five years; yet none of this seems to faze them.

Human beings are a very flawed species. There have been continuous wars since the beginning of time.  The biggest victims of war are ordinary civilians - women and children especially. comments.name: THEODORE MARZILLI

comments.name: Katie
comments.body: Narrative art includes novels, but these objects are not included.  I would love to see a mint, first edition of The Grapes of Wrath. Why not celebrate all versions of narrative art?  Without the words, none of this would exist!

comments.body: When looking at Bond Index funds consider both the share price which can show a gain or a loss, and the total return which includes dividends. Share price * number of shares is the total value of your holding. The share price of bond funds has dropped as interest rates have risen over the last six years. Take Vanguard BND Total US Bond ETF. Looking at the return for last 10 years. The share price high was $89 in July 2020. The price today is  $71.81. About a 14.5% drop. Yikes! But the total return is up 14.25% over that period. That is because interest rates have gone up and reinvested dividends have purchased more shares. Key there is "reinvested". You have not lost anything so long as you have not sold shares. If interest rates drop again the share price will go up but the dividends will be lower. This is for a hypothetical case of purchased shares 10 years ago, held them, value today. But it gives you the picture. You can look up your exact real return or loss at your brokerage. Do not just look at total cost capital gain/loss as that figure includes shares purchased with dividends. An Intermediate term pure Treasury bond fund like VGIT has had a similar drop in share price and a similar positive total return. There is a tax loss harvesting opportunity here. If you are a long term owner of BND or VBTLX you can sell/exchange the shares for VGIT or VBILX. Use the "loss" to offset capital gains from selling some stock fund shares or regular income from interest and dividends.

In 2020, we slashed the maximum allowable sulfur content in marine fuel oil from 3.5% down to just 0.5%. Sulfate aerosols from marine traffic have historically acted as an unintentional planetary cooling shield. Large commercial vessels traditionally burned heavy fuel oil rich in sulfur, which produced immense volumes of sulfur dioxide (SO₂) gas upon combustion. Once in the atmosphere, this gas transformed into highly reflective sulfate particles.

Modeling simulations show that removing sulfate aerosols has added roughly 0.05°C of additional warming to the planet, effectively bringing forward 2 to 3 years of global warming. Maybe we should reverse track and actually increase sulfur content in fuel oil.

That everything Trump does, he does for Putin, is somehow immune from serious discussion in the press. The commentariat here, on the other hand, often draws this inference. It sure seems to be the throughline in all these recent deviations from long-lost norms.

comments.name: mark
comments.body: Keep the Strait closed to Iranian traffic. Get tankers through when you can. Keep improving alternate by-pass routes for oil. Iran and Oman will not control the Strait. It is an international waterway. Hold out for as long as it takes.

comments.name: Christian Haesemeyer
comments.body:
There’s still a shocking lack of honesty in appraisals not just from the administration, but the nominally anti-Trump foreign policy community as well. Iran’s military has not been “weakened” in any real sense, it clearly retains the ability to disrupt US staging and logistics in the Gulf region, endanger civilian traffic through the Straight, and the internal coherence and political loyalty of its armed forces. The three military functions vital to the Iranian strategy have thus not been eliminated or, it appears, even been significantly undermined. It’s of course true that the ongoing conflict inflict further damage on the already strained Iranian economy, but given that U.S./Israel were never going to return any frozen funds or allow sanctions relief in the first place, that isn’t really a point of leverage. (You won’t pay protection if the racketeers end up smashing up your shop anyway every time.)

On the other hand, US force projection in the Middle East has been severely damaged, its naval forces and strategic assets are dangerously overextended, and the global economic and political fallout of this ill-advised war is undermining U.S. influence every day it continues. 

Far from being a”stalemate”, this was is an unmitigated disaster for the US.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body:
Every American in our military harming Iran should be very ashamed of what they are doing, there is no honor in this. In fact it harms US security and it is at the behest of a foreign power. 

Once you are in you are trapped, though one would hope that at least some, those with the most mature consciences, would refuse orders, but it seem to not be a thing. Nobody indoctrinates like the Air Force. I hope potential enlistees are paying attention.

comments.name: Man Ray
comments.body: Why would we expect Iran to negotiate seriously with a pair of real estate investors? It's an insult to the Iranians and a disaster for the Americans. Bring back the experts. We want this over. Now.

comments.name: Abe
comments.body: I am saddened the United States has gotten itself into this silly Benjamin Netanyahu obsession.       Declare victory and pull out.    Iran can rebuild their country with Hormuz tolls.    Iran is not  a threat comparable to the myriad of threats the United States faces, most of them from within.

articles.title: U.S. and Iran Survey the Damage After a Night of Intense Strikes
articles.summary: The American military said its barrage was retaliation against recent attacks on U.S. forces and marine traffic. Iranian officials said a wedding was hit and civilians killed.

comments.name: Monica
comments.body: The whole video thing is so creepy. My neighbors likewise use a doorbell camera that apparently records the entire street - I hear "Hi, you are being recorded" every time I walk by. I think that's highly unusual. And to ask a visitor to be recorded while he's living in your house is weird on a different level. What is it that all these cameras are supposed to be preventing?

comments.name: Vox Pop
comments.body:
"Set Aside an Hour for the Tuna Melt" ...

Similar experience when a friend and I visited a restaurant in Ipswich, MA, a couple of summers ago. It was lovely little place with the porch dining area overlooking great views. 

We were the only guests, and the waiter pitched the Catch of the Day. 

After 45 minutes of waiting, when we asked the waiter to check the status with the kitchen, we were somewhat sheepishly told: "It should be ready in about 10-15 minutes as the Chef had just returned from the local fishery with the catch of the day!"

comments.name: Kate
comments.body: My mom and my father's sister have remained best friends since my parent's divorce in 1985 and after my father's death in 2007. My aunt was my maid of honor at my mom's second wedding. The status of a marriage doesn't dictate the kinds of relationships people are allowed to have who met and formed bonds over family ties, experiences, and children. I am so grateful that these two women kept all of my family in touch with each other over the years.

comments.name: Salix
comments.body:
Re the lake house:
What would be the owner's liability if there was an accident with a guest and the owner was not present. What if a guest plugs in too many appliances, blows a fuse, sparks a fire, etc.?  I would think that her home ownership insurance would look askance at people being there.

comments.name: Kate
comments.body: I have an aunt who got divorced in the last ten years, after being married to her husband for my entire life, and it’s definitely a weird dynamic. Her ex is a very nice man who has always been kind to me, and after I got married he texted me a long message of congratulations and sent me some honeymoon money, which was so much more than I expected and so generous of him! But it does sometimes feel weird, like I’m somehow cheating on my aunt if I have contact with her ex, even if I enjoy talking to him, because she still has animosity towards perceived wrongs and she complains about it to us. Very hard situation to navigate, I empathize with both the writer and her father. I wish I didn’t know anything about their divorce so I could just treat this uncle as an acquaintance without the baggage!

comments.name: Maggie Holder
comments.body: We belong to a house sitting website called TrustedHousesitters.com. There is a requirement for interior cameras to be deactivated when a sitter is occupying the house. Though we like to spy on our cat when we are not home, having a camera in the hallway where someone may be walking to the bathroom in the middle of the night in their pjs, or nothing(!), would be a definite invasion of privacy.

comments.name: Elle
comments.body:
LW1: Nothing wrong with staying in touch and being civil after divorce, many families do that. Expecting to be invited on a trip is too much, but lunch invitation is harmless and not anything you should be managing.  

LW2: I agree with you, you rewarded the service by the waiter, not kitchen staff. $20 might have been too high, but nothing that left you broke. 

LW3: Team nephew. He presented a reasonable solution, accept it or pay for a boarding service.

comments.name: LF
comments.body: This situation is the opposite.  My uncle had an affair and divorced his wife - my "aunt".  It was a very messy situation touching many family members.  40 years later everyone is in touch with our beloved "aunt" and some stay in touch with and forgiven our uncle. Others not so much. It's emotionally hard for our cousins who have a difficult relationship with their father that some family include him and others don't. Split families have a lot of baggage.  I'm sorry for the son who wrote in that he is still embarrassed by his father.  It's hard to let go.

articles.title: Why Does My Divorced Father Keep Reaching Out to My Mother’s Relatives?
articles.summary: A long-divorced father’s wish to stay in the lives of his ex-wife’s family is a source of embarrassment for his middle-aged child.

comments.name: eahostudio
comments.body: Thank you for the well-written and illustrated vacation. I felt like I was with you every step, or chug, of the way. Including cancellation serendipity.

comments.name: Patrick Donovan
comments.body: I loved the mention of Wakefield, R.I., my home for 19 years. "The Hub of South County," as I used to describe it, has everything you need, and my friends at work (I commuted to Providence) were always amused when I would say that I lived where other people vacationed.

comments.name: Philadelphia Lady
comments.body: As a train enthusiast from a young age, who is now pushing 70, this sounds fabulous.

comments.name: William
comments.body:
I am so happy this article appears today!
I am spending my working vacation in Texas. I've lived in Massachusetts all my life but plan to retire here.
I took the train from south station Boston to Longview, Texas. First to Chicago  where we had to wait 4 hours for the second leg to Texas. It was so stressful free and relaxing.  I could read and use my computer. Walk around,stretch. Bring some food of my own. And it makes many stops to get a quick bite in some stations. Like Chicago and the others. It sat for 1 hour in front of the Cardinals stadium.  I could hear the roar of the crowd.  Sunsets are glorious and enjoy seeing signs like Hope Arkansas. Feels nothing like an airport or crazy Ice troops around. And basically I saw a slow tour of New York,Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana,Arkansas Missouri.  I paid extra for the sleeper  and could relax and think in anonymous pleasure.

comments.name: Annette
comments.body: A fun read, thank you! It inspired me to visit and enjoy all the different places you landed in, perhaps next summer.

comments.name: Jay
comments.body: A lovely travelogue.  BUT, after adding up the total cost of the trip—$560 lodging, $490.75 transportation (moped and e-bike included), $202.10 eating, and $9 museum for a total of $1252.85— I think I would drive my car for at least part of that excursion, excluding the ferries. For those on modest working class incomes, such a week end excursion would be an indulgence.

comments.name: ellitpical
comments.body: Just got back from a trip to the Baltics. Obviously entirely using public /private transit. The chaos of running a public travel option within a state seems onerous whereas we traveled in relatively new democracies - the 3 Baltic states are 35 years young) for similar costs as quoted by the author (four hour bus from Tallinn to Riga and another four from Riga to Vilnius. Then back to Tallinn for a 2 hour luxurious ferry ride to Helsinki). No fuss / no cancelations/ clean and courteous all along.

comments.name: Dani W
comments.body: Some of my fondest memories are from a vacation I took in the '90's. I flew into Boston's Logan airport, took the train downtown stayed at the youth hostel there for a week and rode the subway everywhere. Then I took a bus to Provincetown and took the ferry to Cape Cod, where I stayed at another youth hostel and rented a bike and rode all over for 4 or 5 days. Then I took the ferry back to Boston and needed one more night because there was a limit on the number of nights so people I met told me to go to the Irish Embassy. I was like, why the Irish Embassy I'm not Irish and do embassies do that sort of thing? They laughed and told me it was a bar which had an upper floor set up as a hostel as well so I slept in a cot with probably 30 other people, but it was fine.

articles.title: No Car? No Problem: An East Coast Odyssey by Train, Ferry and Bus
articles.summary: A self-described transit romantic set out to visit prime summer destinations using only public transportation. Would getting there really be half the fun?

articles.title: Bernie, AOC and Bannon Can Agree on One Thing: the Fight Against Data Centers
articles.byline: Amrith Ramkumar, Eliza Collins and Anthony DeBarros
articles.summary: The strange political bedfellows are warning about the risks of the AI build-out, an issue animating the left and the right.

comments.name: David Harris
comments.body:
Everyone should do a simple Google search.  "How many data centers are currently near me?"  Mine came up 218 within 20 miles.  At no point have they ever bothered anyone  or has anyone been aware that they were here already.  

The backlash to these is incredibly self destructive.  China must be laughing about this.

comments.name: David Yastrab
comments.body:
Anything Bannon, AOC and Sanders agree on is toxic to the country. Shooting ourselves in the foot by stopping data center construction while the rest of the world embraces AI seems backwards and right up their alley.

AI is here. It's not going away. We need to lead the world in technology, not wait and then wonder what happened.

comments.name: CONRAD VONBLANKENBURG
comments.body: Data centers are just another racket. They allow and contribute to people "WASTING" TIME AND MONEY. THE DAMAGE COMMUNITIES AND RIP OFF INVESTORS.

comments.name: Michael Gaffney
comments.body:
How do you do a story like this and not say what Bannon doesn't like about them? You gave a quote saying "We have to get this right" but what are the ramifications of getting it wrong? What are Bannon's definitions of "right" and "wrong". If he is against them because he fears the electrical and water usage, is he still unhappy with the centers that will use closed loop cooling and BYOP?

⭐I cannot recommend.

comments.name: Robert Sartini
comments.body: If Data Centers generate their own power and recycle water they should be allowed.  Just not in the meadow next to my house.

comments.name: Mitchell Ross
comments.body: I don't think government should subsidize data centers, but why ban them - as long as they have their own power sources (or contribute to existing ones), and recycle their water ? For cooling alternatives to water - how about deep geothermal heat pumps ? Otherwise they seem like good neighbors paying taxes and thus helping out a community. Or what am I missing ?

comments.name: Richard Gamer
comments.body:
This reminds me of the convergence of the Tea Party and the Occupy Wall Street Movement. They hated each other but hated DC/Wall Street intrigues even more. 

However, this could be the pivotal issue that re-unites the nation. So, how about this for the 2028 presidential tickets:

Republican - Bannon/Ocasio-Cortez

Democratic - Ocasio-Cortez/Bannon

comments.name: philip jennings
comments.body: AI gets smarter every day.  How can the US enact restrictions on data centers and AI when other countries inevitably refuse to follow our  lead?

comments.name: lowcountry ike
comments.body: I love her voice, which does write a music of its own as she performs, and her point-of-view definitely does ricochet around in the lower reaches of the spaced-out blue-collar working-class universe, which has just as many stars and comets as any other, but too much of her stuff is built on the lowest common denominator and the rest relies on a persona that for now at least is her real bread and butter. I was hoping she would make me laugh at loud.

comments.name: SN
comments.body: Discovered her on Netflix. LOVE her show. The writing is funny in a smooth way. It's very relatable. Leanne herself is a natural. I love the cast of this show. They all are very talented and natural actors. Highly recommend it.

comments.name: Lief Mialone
comments.body:
I tell my Students that if you've become Jaded or forgotten why you Loved something, to Watch a Woman do almost anything. 
And like Sophie Cunningham or Coco Gauf, Ms. Morgan reminds us that when Craft meets Voice, we become undeniably True and enduringly Powerful.. 
And though like Roseanna and Phyllis Diller before her Leanne's core Theme is to endure and overcome HER Family too, that's what her Audience connects to and craves  amidst the universal Tropes of Marriage and Motherhood. 
For ultimately, that how "Others" find both Audience and Voice within Comedy's evolution from the Voices of mainstream Men like Newhart, Seinfeld and Bargatze. Leanne Morgan's power is born of familiarity but her Glory in Transcending "just" Motherhood and Spousal indignities is that she is ordinally Powerful and that is a Universal Voice that irresistibly  draws us all to her emergence

comments.name: Eva G.
comments.body: I came across her videos during Covid.  She was a breath of fresh air and funny as heck. I shared her videos on my FB page and would make all of my friends watch. Young, old, men, women. They all loved her too.  She has that Dolly Parton quality about her. She is just delightful no matter what she is saying.  A light in a sometimes dim world.  You go girl!  P.S. "doo doo balls" is a must watch.

comments.name: Dude
comments.body: She is charmingly (very) funny.

comments.name: Vivian
comments.body: Love her!

comments.name: TF
comments.body: I recently discovered Leanne. I immediately loved her because she reminds me of the women in my family. My grandmothers and their daughters all had a kind of country humor that Leanne easily possesses. They tease, gab, flatter, gossip, and all love a good story that is always intended to make you giggle or laugh and learn something about someone. Men are the target of much of the teasing. There is a kind of tell all in the conversation, which reinforces the bonds. I grew up in Texas and the accent is somewhat like Leanne, though hers is more pronounced. My family would mimic accents and use those deeper Southern drawls to emphasize humor. When I moved from Texas to the MA in the 90s I missed that gabby fun that was the social core of my upbringing. I later moved to California where, unfortunately, it seems to be missing altogether. It's rare to find anyone, except with those from the South, who talks story. As evidenced by Leanne's success, it may be what America is missing.

comments.name: Brad Steel
comments.body: She's a breath of fresh air to an art form that needs it. She is an American treasure.

articles.title: Maybe Leanne Morgan Can Heal America
articles.summary: The homey Southern comic is a red-state phenomenon with blue-state celebrity, big tours, a Netflix series and Judd Apatow’s adoration. How did she get here?

comments.name: Cece
comments.body: My family of origin knows what ooflay ooflays are, and p-o-a-c, and night night pat pat bye bye. When my partner asks for my help, I ask “what’s it worth to you?” And she says “a lot”, I say “OK”. Now my grandson has learned it. Familect is fun.

comments.name: Daryn Eller
comments.body: I suggest reading Natalia Ginzberg's Family Lexicon, devoted to the topic, and also an incredible accounting of living under fascism in pre- and wartime Italy.

comments.name: Susan Koop
comments.body: Our neighbor recently told her husband from her kitchen window that Indy (our dog) and Dave were coming down the street. He asked her who Indian Dave was. Guess whose nickname is now Indian Dave? Outsiders are puzzled.

comments.name: PFD
comments.body: The funniest word in out familect is TIBO from a sign my two daughters drove by when teens.—Total Inventory Blow Out— a term to describe what is also known in our family as poopdiarrhea.

comments.name: Laura
comments.body: Our family favorite is when our daughter was about 4 and had diarrhea and she came out of the bathroom and said "I throwed up out my butt".  Ever since that is our diagnosis for diarrhea.

comments.name: DD
comments.body: And we had a family whistle  - a short singular  tune that spanned 3 generations, gathering the tribe and corraling  errant kids.....

comments.name: Preglad
comments.body: Ammuinu is a southern Italian dialect term for confusion or excess noise. I my extended Sicilian family, it somehow got further transitioned to citamonia. Another such further variation of street lingo is "Ma k air doo keestu kha" which is built on "Ma che è succiuto?". What in the name of heaven (or hell) is going on?". Either of these, (or countless other gems dramatically poised in despairing or amazed tones) with accompanying gestures, can serve as whatever gathering's show stoppers.

comments.name: Margaret
comments.body:
Years ago I heard a story about two hispanic house cleaner sisters whose kids were watched by two Vietnamese sisters while they worked. Neither spoke much of the others language, so a few times a day, when the hispanic sisters would call to check on the kids, the call would consist of "Baby ok?" and the reply "Baby ok."

I can't count the number of times my kids and I have checked on each other with "Baby ok? "Baby ok."

articles.title: Every Family Has Its Own Private Language. What Does That Tell Us About Ourselves?
articles.summary: “Familects” emerge out of in-jokes and mispronunciations, but they reveal something about how all language evolves.

articles.title: There Are Four Forces Pressuring Bonds: War Is No. 1
articles.byline: Jack Pitcher, Shradha Dinesh and Ryan Dezember
articles.summary: Fiscal worries, a new Federal Reserve chairman and even the flood of AI bonds are helping drive the recent climb in yields.

comments.name: DUANE SMITH
comments.body: Just how was the #1 cause determined, and on what evidence?

comments.name: Toni Tavric
comments.body:
Latest Fox News Regime TV poll : 71% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living

Yessir , 71% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Even Fox News Regime TV admits it.

comments.name: Edward Horkan
comments.body: The article said that publicly held debt as a portion of GNP is approaching levels not seen since WWII.  Actually such debt is already at levels not seen since then.  It is approaching record levels.  But the debt is in fact a much greater burden than it was 80 years ago for at least two reasons.  First the World War II debt was at minimal interest rates because Americans were patriotically willing to buy war bonds with a very low return.  Second, the cause for large borrowing ended with the war.  People rightly anticipated that the government would soon have low deficits or even a surplus in the near future.  Now interest rates are back to normal and the federal deficit is projected to get substantially worse over time.

comments.name: Patrick C
comments.body: This is absurd, the market reacts with elation on one little comment from a Fed Gov. while the fundamentals remain unchanged: oil over $90, crack spreads at record highs, refinery infrastrucutre damaged for years ahead, and zero material progress towards a solution. The dip buyers have been inflating this things two fold but there is just so much liquidity out there who knows where the ceiling is!?

comments.name: Christophoros P
comments.body: Actually there are five forces - you omitted Trump’s sheer stupidity in any and all economic matters

comments.name: Toni Tavric
comments.body: Trump wears a wig. Pass it on.

comments.name: David O
comments.body: Funny that the chart showing fuel prices doesn’t go back all the way back to 2022.

comments.name: Stephen S S Hyde
comments.body:
I'm wondering how much another factor may be raising long bond yields, the risk to foreign holders that the US won't ultimately pay up. Improbable, you say? Tell that to the Russians. 

Cheers, Steve

comments.name: Dr B
comments.body: Why does the world continue to do business with Russia, and why do any institutions permit Russians to participate in any international forum?

comments.name: Lake Monster
comments.body:
Find the Russian factories and supply chains and destroy them.  

Do it again and again and again.

comments.name: Mark Keil
comments.body: this development may sound familiar to survivors of the London blitz when the Germans developed the V2 rockets, replacing the earlier, slower and noisier V1's.

comments.name: FZ
comments.body: Russia cannot defeat Ukraine. Ukraine cannot defeat Russia. This is Iran-Iraq war redux.

comments.name: christopher
comments.body: It would be helpful to add some sort of estimate for the cost of the jet powered drone beyond a link to a Russian language Telegram message.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: I wonder if the best way to respond to this new threat is to locate the sites where these drones are assembled and then bomb them relentlessly.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
I think shooting down the jet powered drones is a second step. 
First step is to interrupt the production of them. 
Find the key part(s) manufacture(s) and bomb them.

comments.name: Rick Morris
comments.body: Iran has jet powered drones that were used very effectively against US military installations in the present conflict. Ukraine will respond to the new Russian threat not only with defensive measures but jet powered drones of its own. Mass attacks using hundreds of these weapons is the face of aerial warfare in the future. I can only hope that our inept Sec of Defense understands that.

articles.title: The New Jet-Powered Drones That Are Breeding Anxiety in Ukraine
articles.summary: These Russian drones are more destructive, faster and harder to shoot down than the propeller-driven models that Moscow has used throughout the war.

comments.name: Guitarman
comments.body: For many years I was taking Doxylamine to help with sleep. It may have helped somewhat. I take a number or prescriptions for blood pressure control so decided to discontinue Doxylamine. I have struggle most nights with long term insomnia and have on occasion taken Doxylamine Succinate 25mg. It works well but I am very tired  in the morning and usually have to go back to bed for additional sleep time. I have Magnesium Oxide 250mg that I will try tonight in the hope that it will help my long term insomnia and constipation. A recent lab test at the E.R.  indicated that my magnesium was low. I was given it by I.V. I don't want to alter the delicate balance of my chemistry. The E.R. were looking for the cause of diarrhea, that I suspected was caused by eating tainted raspberries and lettuce weeks ago. Stool samples were negative. I hope that my biochemistry is now back to normal.

comments.name: mo
comments.body: I take both melatonin and magnesium at night. My sleep became seriously disordered when I started menopause. The combo has made a significant difference in my ability to get good sleep. I've been doing this for a few years, with no adverse effects.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body: I've been taking 1000 mg for years, to prevent foot cramps.  It does nothing for my sleep, with which I have problems often.

comments.name: Bern
comments.body: I take magnesium for other reasons. Now I'll take it at night!

comments.name: LAJ
comments.body: I use it to avoid cramps at night, it does that, so it gives me better sleep. The better sleep is just a side effect of not waking at night with cramps.

comments.name: esp
comments.body: It certainly is better for pooping and pooping.  I was on it as a prescription for low magnesium.  They had to take me off it.

comments.name: txmd
comments.body: Poorly absorbed magnesium causes diarrhea.  not so good for sleep..

comments.name: Joan Wood
comments.body: Why wasn’t info shared in this article  on foods high in magnesium?

articles.title: Is Magnesium the New Melatonin?
articles.summary: The supplement is rising in popularity among those hunting for better sleep. We asked experts whether the science justifies the hype.

comments.name: rf
comments.body: I also had an Oma and Opa, They were Hitler refugees from Danzig, arriving in NYC with my mom and aunt in 1939. Opa was born in Russia and Oma in northern Germany. My fondest childhood memories were of Oma, who loved me unconditionally. She died in 1972, Opa in 1986 and there are only a very few people who knew them personally. RIP to mine and yours.

comments.name: Connie
comments.body: Last December, I listed my family "camp" on a lake in the Ocala Forest of Central Florida.  Purchased in 1958 by my parents and aunt/uncle when I was 9yrs old, it had been abandoned since 1964 when my father died.  The Airstream trailer rotted away as did the dock that Daddy and Uncle Jim built .  When the land passed to me in 1998, I let it lay until 2025 when I decided to clean it up and sell it.  I just turned down a good offer, $10K over its value.  It is hard to explain why I did that but I think you know.

comments.name: Ken M
comments.body: As the song lyric goes “you don’t know what you’ve got ‘til it’s gone”

comments.name: Megan
comments.body: What a lovely article!  I, too, like many of the readers' comments here relate to the special memories from grandparents' homes.  I can still see in my memories exactly how all the rooms were laid out in the farmhouse and fondly remember the last time I stayed on the farm with my grandmother a little over 20 years ago before she moved to an assisted living.  I dreamed more than one dream of that house and the memories in the subsequent years.  My cousin remodeled it and updated it, and when I visited and was in it, it helped not seeing the same house.  It made it easier to realize it's the memories that remain and are carried with you.  But I must admit, every time I open my spice cabinet I can smell the rich aromas of cinnamon, nutmeg and others spices from the wooden rack I brought from the basement kitchen, and it brings back the summer memories when my cousins and I played restaurant in the basement.

comments.name: globe
comments.body: I had a special experience after visiting the family cemetery. I drove back to the street of my first childhood home nearby. There were a lot of new fences separating the scenic backyards, which are jarring. However in the front yard, under a large tree, a young girl and her father were raking leaves.  It was like looking at my father and myself so many years ago. The feeling was both bittersweet and oddly comforting.  I also realized the dad was foreign born and this was his only child, a societal change from the 1950s when the block had large families. On that visit I connected with my life and the changes in American society over decades.

comments.name: David
comments.body: This column really struck home, my father died last year and my mother three years ago. We spent many happy times at family cottages over the years but unfortunately when our loved ones die  we realize that it was them that made it special not the cottage. Our current cottage is still used but the feeling is different, the memories are there as reminders but there is an emptiness and loss of soul that is striking. It will probably be sold next year and with it our family gathering space. Buildings do not make happy memories but the people who live within and share their love and laughter and simple joy at being together in the midst of rejuvenating , eternal nature.

comments.name: arboretum
comments.body: I spent six weeks every summer, for six years, at my grandparents home in rural Kentucky. The rest of the year I lived in Europe. I reflect on the juxtaposition of these two experiences and enjoyed both, but in fact, those FREE six weeks every year were some of the best memories I have. I will always love my grandparents for their loving, kind, understanding, and forgiving attitudes. They died more than 35 years ago but I hope to create these same kinds of experiences for my own grandchildren. It’s not the place, but the love.

comments.name: AE
comments.body:
What my grandparents home held for me, was intolerable to lose so I bought it after my grandmother passed. I lived in another state though had dreams and a plan to restore and return to summer there. Then life kept happening. I tend to visit living relatives and spent little time just visiting the memories in the empty (of grandparents), home. Truth be told, THEY made the home, logically, but…

All of this said, I feel for you, tremendously. When I decided to sell, it was much more difficult to sign my name than could have been reasonable. The buyers could not have been more patient. I was signing away part of the place that was and always will be, home. I still visit friends out there on occasion, and always pass the house my grandfather built and is still standing, so strong.

articles.title: Selling My Grandparents’ Home Is Like Losing Them Again
articles.summary: A plot of land was the last thing connecting us to my grandparents.

comments.name: julie
comments.body:
Wow. What a fantastic tribute, obit. I love reading the obits section, learning about prople’s lives and accomplishments. In that regard…

this is the best obit I’ve read about any musician. 

Wish I’d seen her live and heard more of her music while she was in this body. Going to look for it now.

comments.name: David
comments.body: Beautiful obituary for an amazing artist.  I was lucky to see her perform twice - both times were transcendent.

comments.name: nzierler
comments.body: A wonderful voice that I first had the pleasure of hearing at a jazz club in Manhattan in 1986. I have all her albums and I am saddened by her passing.

comments.name: Roman
comments.body: First time I heard Miss Wilson's voice I was smitten. Not being much of a music category guy myself I was taken by her choice of material and her unwillingness to cover the same old stuff. Attacking the music of Robert Johnson and The Monkees pretty much sold me even before hearing a note....and then that gorgeous voice. comments.body: It is difficult to argue against the core issues this letters is addressing. Grade inflation has been a significant  issue for the last few decades and schools have failed to address it. Admission is still biased although in different ways than in the past. Legacy admissions are still going strong. Schools depend on private donors with strings attached that are not necessarily in the interest of unbiased education and research. comments.name: LF

ok, let's assume "merit based" is a prime criterion for admission. How is merit defined?  

Surely not just because you graduated from a tony private school for the privileged few, unless your grades were better than, say, those of an applicant from a public high school. Surely not because you or your family are well enough off to pay full freight, no need for scholarships or loans. Surely not because a relative graduated at some point ahead of you, or your relative can endow the college with a new football stadium. Surely not because of your gender or race. Surely not because you're a fantastic athlete who can help the university win games and bring in more revenue, as it is not the prime role of higher education to produce olympic-level  athletes.  

If admission is based on merit, the individual has a proven record of scholastic achievement and potential to excel and is a well rounded, stable individual likely to succeed if admitted as a student, what will our colleges look like?   

If neither race nor gender is considered (remember no diversity criteria will be tolerated), if neither wealth nor privilege is considered because wealth is not merit,  universities will almost certainly be majority female and with an over-representation of Asian students, and fewer white men. When my baby was 2 weeks old, postpartum depression kicked in hard.  I tried to get help, but my husband didn't get it.  My OB/ GYN prescribed a low dose of and SSRI, and I made the earliest appt with a psychiatrist I could find - 6 weeks out. It got worse quickly, and a week or so later I begged my husband to come home from work and take me to the emergency room.  They doubled my medication, prescribed more, I spoke with a psychiatrist, and they set up more psych visits sooner. I wanted them to admit me, so I could sleep, but they wouldn't.  Twenty years later, I look back and see this more clearly - in addition to the hormonal changes, my husband had refused to hire any help.  We had no family nearby- at all - and he wouldn't allow even a part time nanny, thinking that I should be able to do all of it and we couldn't afford it. I had never seen this in him during the long time we'd known each other. Now, we're divorced, and our 20 year old son is thriving, but I still can't believe I survived it.  No one should ever have to go through this kind of isolation, especially when caring for a another human being.  

Why did my husband act this way?  Internalized stigma of mental illness, handed down to him by his old-school Brooklyn parents.

To the women out there getting married and starting families  - always have a savings account that can get you out of immediate danger.  I did not.

We cannot do it. It is up to the Iranian people to do it. Obviously, with our assistance it may be possible, and hopefully Mossad and the CIA are on the ground now to coordinate the effort and supply the means. Sec. Bessent is doing all that is in his control, and those who oppose us (the Russians and Chinese) are doing all that they can as well.

But it will come down to the Iranian people and shedding the necessary blood. It will be a messy struggle and many will die, but the IRGC and their fellow travelers have no compunction whatsoever to do what they must to maintain power. They have built their entire lives on maintaining the regime, and they owe their entire existence on its continuance. And they know that should the regime fall, the repercussions for them will be catastrophic.

It is not at all far-fetched to believe that Iran may become the next Libya, driven by tribal factions and rife with civil war and economic instability for years. Iran still has strong tribal influences even as it has been a unified country for decades. And, as such, it may become a terror hotbed as the need for revenge against the US and Israel may be strong.

comments.body:
We have to give up this obsession with “regime change.” Back in the 20th century, we largely tried it via CIA-sponsored coups—sometimes augmented by military force, as in Vietnam—in the fight against communist governments supported by the then Soviet Union. Now in the 21st century, we’ve been increasingly using military force—sometimes supplemented by boots on the ground and prolonged occupation, as in Afghanistan and Iraq—to fight against Islamic terror groups in many Middle Eastern and African countries. Even when our military has successfully deposed a dictator, as in Venezuela, there has been no concomitant “regime change.”

 

“Regime change” as an objective makes us appear like the western European imperialist nations of the past and presidential pronouncements like “to the victor go the spoils,” make it all the more unpalatable as a reason to go to war. So, if Barton Swaim is right when he suggests that the “regime change” objective for Iran is back on the table, then our history with this objective suggests we are in it for the long haul with an uncertain outcome.

While I regard notions of divinity and divine intervention as highly unlikely,  I was discomforted by the many comments taking this tragedy as an opportunity to prosthelytize their anti-deist views.

Such widespread destruction from natural disasters seems to be on the rise. It is something I fear in my home town which has been destroyed by storms and earthquakes three times in the past. Perhaps the survival of the green house is a testament to good building practices. When I discussed construction with local experts and town officials I was told that good building practices and regulations are pretty much universal and I witnessed the strong reinforcement of the construction I had done. Unfortunately, safety takes a lower priority for many people whose priority need is a roof over your head and protection from the elements at minimal cost. Safety and permanence are an extra cost that many just can’t afford on their own. Not because they are frivolous spenders or lazy, most are hard working people who just don’t get paid enough to afford anything more. It seems to me that allowing this situation is just another expression of humanity’s failure to take responsibility for the precious resources that sustain us, whether it be the environment or the legions of people that make our lifestyles possible.

I audibly gasped when I saw the picture of Rafael Viñoly’s proposed latticework towers. I'm one of many New Yorkers who has avoided Ground Zero for reasons I cannot put into words -- but I would go there to stand witness if those proposed latticework towers had been built.

That day is indelible -- the sky so blue, the air so clean, the temperature so perfect, the images of women walking, carrying their high heeled work shoes as they themselves were barefoot, walking north with the blankest of looks on their faces. 

I remember an older Asian man, in a window of a small dry cleaning shop on the Upper West Side, furiously ironing something as hundreds of people slowly and silently passed by. I wondered why he was so intent on ironing on that day. 

I can't believe it's been 25 years. I still wonder about him.

comments.name: Alphonso Bedoya
comments.body:
Folks forget that one of the reasons-for-being of the original World Trade Center was to revive Downtown Manhattan commercial development, which had migrated to Midtown after the Depression and WWII. 

The towers suffered a high vacancy rate for years— and were largely occupied by government agencies— until conditions actually did revive over a decade after they were built.

Personally, I thought— along with others, including Ellsworth Kelly— after the attack that the whole site should be left a park… in my case, at or a little above street level with shallow pools (where the towers had been) with glazed bottoms to act as huge skylights over an 80-foot-high memorial space on the base of the “Bathtub.” 

But other sensiblities actually submitted proper proposals and we have what we have today.

Arad’s memorial, at least far exceeds my imagination…

Cities are what they are… and memorial structures and spaces within them are wildly varied in impact and appropriateness— Victor Emmanuel’s in Rome, Lenin’s in Moscow, Jefferson’s in D.C.

It’s tempting to let that last example just hang there; but Arad’s design and Arlington Cemetery are stark contrasts to other development in the nation’s capital.

1. Have a long conversation w your daughter about her best friend’s drinking. Tell her of your thinking about contacting her friend’  parents.

4,  assess the danger for your daughter. Does she drive with her while she is drunk?  Who drives?  If you suspect a risk to your daughter then you may have to throw caution over to the necessity of  your daughter’s safety. 
5.  Do you have any solid relationship w your daughter’s friend or her parents? Are they able to take in that kind of information.

As part of that conversation, LW should try to learn more about her home life (if the girl will share). Are her parents abusive or merely strict? Would they support treatment or insist on punishment? The answers could help clarify the next steps. 

One important consideration here is that early intervention can be invaluable. Even if the parents aren't informed, it's possible LW could help arrange a qualified counselor or connect her with AA meetings focused on older teens (they exist).

That's if it is alcoholism. My daughter had friends in college who drank a lot, sometimes to blackout. So did I. I remember waking up with vomit on my bed from my roommate in the bunk above me. As far as I know my daughter's friends and mine eventually found their way out of it. But it's especially scary at this high schooler's age, and shouldn't be ignored.

I also used some networking tools to investigate the promoters.

The IP of the webserver was clearly a spoof off a Cloudflare IP block, the domain name registration was deficient, and the nameserver information also deficient.   A simple Traceroute to the webserver was still going at over 65 hops when i stopped it.  This is all easy to spot and can only be the result of deliberate obfuscation.

Google's response to me was they had looked at the product, the company, and their own ToS and requirements advertisers for not doing consumer harm and concluded that the product advertising was not a problem and would continue.  

As I mentioned above, no such product, or even close to it exists.  The products you see are fabrications with onboard systems that make it appear as though the product has huge storage capacity, but in fact offer maybe 2 TB at best and wil destroy your data if you use them.

Google relies on the appearance of things looking legitimate.

Raised in part by feminist grandparents, who came of age in the roaring 20s in NYC, I felt "liberated" all my life, but recognized that the world pushed back harder against me for that. 

I recognized early on that not me, but the world had to change.  In one interview (L.S.E.) I was asked if I planned to marry (I had 4 A-level exams), since giving me a place would deprive a man, a breadwinner. I honestly replied that I never planned to marry but would support myself. My class contained a handful of women. We banded together.

In my first year at uni, in the 70s, I became familiar with the feminist movement and attended meetings to help change the system, but was discouraged by the dismissive attitude toward beautiful women; those who refused the uniform of revolution embraced at the time, which was a man's tailored suit; and the prudish attitude which denigrated those who expressed lust for the opposite sex (my Sapphic inclined sisters were considered ipso facto more liberated) Dressing down, looking dowdy, seemed to signify that we weren't "objects" to the leaders of the movement at the time. 

Critics accused Steinem and Germaine Greer of succeeding not on their merits but on their attractiveness. They steered the movement away from the forces of dowdy, stern prudishness.

I worked in film for years and the main thing that people on a film set cared about was making the director or the famous actors happy, spoiling them.  An indie director who recently became well-known and just released their third film was someone I knew when they were coming up through the industry. I was also trying to get a film made. This person worked at a place that helped indie filmmakers.  Even though it was their job to help me, they seemed more interested in their own career - themselves... and now they have their career making films, their main goal. Normal in the industry. Big talk about changing things, but ultimately it was about their own career. 
Films & stories are great but in the current climate careers & money are really what's being generated. comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body: There is a surprising omission in this article, both in the text and the photos. The Delhi Metro has proceeded quickly, in large part, because of a brute-force approach that eschews expensive tunnelling in favour of enormous raised railways running down the centre of urban highways. These are held up by immense piers, or you might call them concrete pylons. Each normal pier is about as wide as a small car, but rises three or more storeys above the road - and there are hundreds and hundreds of them dotting the city, with a huge rail deck (viaduct) above every one. I have not been able to find reliable figures, but my guess is that half or even two-thirds of the network has been built on this approach. While I am an admirer of the system overall, and am in awe of how quickly it has been built, readers should be aware that the urban landscape of Delhi has been dramatically overshadowed - quite literally - by these vast concrete behemoths snaking through it. The visual impact has been enormous. If older and more self-conscious cities tried to adopt this cost-effective approach, my prediction is that there would be outrage.

comments.name: Balthazar
comments.body:
This article seems to cast aspersions on the authenticity of Kusama's later work. Why? 

As for artists managing and producing works to their specifications, though the author for some reason cites only Jeff Koons, anyone who has taken a basic art history course knows of the Baroque and Renaissance workshop system by which works were produced collaboratively with the input of many specialists under the management of a single master, to whom the work was attributed. Try googling the "lone genius" myth, a concept which emerged during the Enlightenment. 

The author also impugns Kusama's capacity to make decisions about her practice on her own, especially in her later years. What's at the bottom of these suspicions? 

Kusama was a successful artist who not only was always forthright about her mental illness, she plainly cited it as the reason for her compulsion to create, to externalize her inner life in the form of aesthetic objects. Her work resonated with a wide audience, and she managed to make a lot of money. 

But this article, though no evidence is provided, seems to want us to doubt that she didn't so much as create her own works herself, and that others secretly managed decisions about its production without her involvement. Why? This is a familiar way of undermining or diminishing a successful woman by questioning her agency, authorship, and legitimacy.

comments.name: Quantum Universe

Big Picture: I’m a bit skeptical that the AI infrastructure is definitely a traditional market bubble. 

Yes, it’s an astonishing amount of investment spending but what’s being built are transformative technologies. And not every company involved will land in the multi-winners circle - many will and many won’t. But AI and other forms of advanced computing are likely not going to dissipate as if they’re the tech industry’s and adjacent industries’ equivalent of a fashion trend. 

My hunch: more likely (probability-wise) is that after several years, capex spending and borrowed funding will level off into manageable phases supportive of maintenance, replacement and somewhat routine growth to institute evolutionary adoption of improved designs of hardware, software, connectivity and services. 

While the above is playing out, NOW is the time to consider what strong guardrails need to be deployed (and how & when) regarding the AI realm, including in what manner and where AI centers are deployed.  And to figure out who the guardians might best be and the extent to which regulatory requirements, norms and ethics are established and enforced. 

As part of these developments, serious attention is also needed to ensure the benefits of AI are reasonably and fairly shared broadly across populations and don’t end up essentially in the hands of a comparatively tiny handful of people. 

All of the above is characterized not as a firm prediction but as possible scenarios to be considered.

              History will show, I think, that Ms. Steinem was the single most important reason the New York media sold her version of reality to the American people.   She became a fashionable icon on the grand scale and she made a large part of the future of his time by making sure that the American people were massively catechized on the issue of abortion.  Again, her equally massive influence on the New York media counted for much of that.  They adopted her views, lock stock and barrel.

George Washington fought in many battles and was never wounded. Is Diamond really going to suggest that if Washington had died in the French and Indian War it wouldn't have mattered much? Really?!? Without Washington the Americans very likely would have lost the American Revolution, in which case North American and world history would have been very different.

I think Diamond has it exactly wrong. History is chaotic! Like a ball bouncing down a rocky slope, every rock it hits has the potential to send the ball off in totally different directions -- directions that depend on exactly how the ball hits the rock. Averages do matter of course. Statistically when it reaches the bottom the ball is more likely to come to rest in the middle of the slope than on the extreme left or right. But any result is possible, and every rock the ball hits matters. Every French musketeer who took aim at Washington could have changed the course of history had his aim been a little better. It's the butterfly effect. Any small change today could eventually have great consequences in the future.

Thank you, Mr. Jones.  

For raising a banner as it were and reminding us:  that yes!  

People DO matter.  People are NOT simply pawns and chess pieces moving around on a board--

--shoved about by economic forces or the weather.  

Naturally (as a Christian) i bridle at this rather curt dismissal of Jesus Christ.  I would insist:  no.  He was NOT simply a remarkably charismatic figure (among many)--

--who had the good fortune to be embraced by a Saint Paul. 

Read the four gospels.  And (among many things) note the exclamation that came so many times. 

"No man ever spoke like this man."  He spoke with authority.  An authority that enabled Him to say:  pay attention, folks.  I'm telling you the way it ought to be.  

Remember the lines from Gray's Elegy?  

            "Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest.
              Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood."

Horsefeathers! cried American journalist and gadfly, H. L. Mencken.  

"The test of a Milton is that he function like a Milton."  

Which would be my retort to Mr. Diamond.  Lively and engaging though he is.  

You speak of other "great men" waiting in the wings, should the genuine "great man" fail for some reason to show up.  

Produce the doughty guy that would have won the Battle of Agincourt, had there been no Henry V.

comments.name: OD

There are few instances of leaders making things dramatically better, but single individuals, given great power, have often made them worse.

One such would be Henry V, whose reign is described here as a "rip-roaring success". He restarted the 100 Years War after 30 years of truce. 

England lost that second, final round of the Hundred Years War even more comprehensively than it had the first, losing vast lands it had held for centuries. 

True, England's defeat came after Henry's death, but he made it inevitable. His fight was carried on by his very capable brother John. But the job was impossible. England lost the first phase of the war despite winning key battles at Crecy and Poitiers. It lost the second phase despite winning key battles at Agincourt and Verneuil. That tells you: France was unconquerable by England. Smart people had drawn that lesson at the end of phase 1 around 1380.

Henry's disastrous war impoverished England, and its failure sparked the Wars of the Roses. So while England and France had enjoyed comparable power and prestige when Henry was crowned, by 1500 France was well on the way to superpower status while England was a backwater.

Already within a few years of Henry V's death, almost all of his victories had been wiped away by someone who really does provide backing for the Great (Wo)Man theory of history. Someone who came from nowhere, with everything stacked against her, and changed history through sheer guts and determination: Joanne of Arc.

The article does not, in my opinion, adequately inform readers about—or fully grasp—the depth and potential danger of the current Spanish situation, not only for Spain itself but also for Europe and, perhaps, beyond.
I would urge The Times and its correspondents to read books and newspapers representing all sides of Spanish life and thought, and to listen to people from across the political and cultural spectrum. Spain is a very old, complex country, and too often The Times seems to approach it with its conclusions already formed rather than with a genuinely open mind.
This is one of the reasons why, during the past few years, I have come very close to canceling my subscription. The many other excellent sections of the newspaper have so far stopped me from doing so.
I hope that by the time we finally reach 2028, The Times will have returned to something closer to normal—and that what sometimes feels like “The Trump Gazette” will have disappeared for good.

As a Spanish reader of The New York Times, I always read its articles about Spain with interest, and I am consistently struck by how positively the country — and, more specifically, its government — tends to be portrayed.
In this case, I was surprised by the reporter’s approval of the willingness shown by some of our politicians to welcome the growing presence of Chinese companies in Spain. Here, it is widely known that this favourable attitude is largely connected to the role played by our former prime minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, who has acted as a lobbyist for the Chinese government and Chinese companies. Zapatero — whom Americans may also know because of his controversial ties to Venezuela — is currently facing scrutiny over allegations involving corruption and money laundering. It would be good to see The New York Times report on these aspects of Spain as well. When might we expect an article examining the less flattering side of Pedro Sánchez’s government?
I also found it interesting that the reporter described Spain by saying, “This is a place that feels like it’s moving forward,” when the general perception here is precisely the opposite. The country is moving backwards by virtually every measure that directly affects people’s prosperity, with real wages stagnant or even declining for almost twenty years. And that is without even mentioning democratic standards or the rampant corruption affecting the parties that govern us — all of them, without exception.

Each of us then chose to role play a pivotal figure in the Women's liberation movement as a  part of our presentation.  
We then role-played the points and the rationale that best represented the perspective of key leaders of the Women's liberation movement. I proudly researched and then represented Gloria Steinem 's  views.

Slacklining as a senior might sound too challenging for most of us, but research shows a basic level of balance is crucial for healthy aging.

A 2024 Ontario study of nearly 100,000 adults aged 66 or older found that survival was substantially reduced after hip fractures, especially among older men. 

Fewer than one-third of the men and about half of the women were alive five years after a hip fracture.

Further to that, a major Cochrane review found that exercise focused primarily on balance and functional movements reduced the total rate of falls by 24%.

Not all falls are due to balance issues – low blood pressure, poor vision, peripheral neuropathy, and of course cognitive decline – can all contribute to falls. 

But for most people, basic balance training as we age can pay some big fall-proofing dividends.
